en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 30 [Tibetan & Sanskrit 33] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[1195] Now I shall explain another sequence of rites for the Buddha-Ḍāka, according to the previously mentioned Buddha-Ḍāka and the sequences of the Āgamas and so forth.
Without the Āgama, a yogin shall not become a Buddha-kaula. One should not abandon the method of the Āgamas, nor should one abandon that which is born of the Three Jewels.
I go for refuge eternally to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Relying upon the perfection of wisdom, the accomplishment of yoga is achieved.
By means of the yoga of instantaneous form, one should contemplate one’s own body as blue,
fierce, deformed, and wrathful— inspiring fear even in the fearful.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, with the moon bound as a crest upon his matted locks,
with a mass of matted hair containing the universal vajra, adorned with a garland of skulls,
complete with all ornaments, and possessing a body endowed with the six mudrās— BAṂ HŪṂ.
Clad in a tiger skin, comfortably seated in the half-lotus posture,
possessing three eyes and a fierce form, with four necks and four faces,
endowed with twelve arms, he is the supreme gnosis of emptiness.
The garland of the heads of all the wicked is a wreath produced at the time of universal dissolution;
it is the face of Kleśabhairava, trampled upon by the feet of all the wicked.
Envy, having fallen into thirst and delusion, is downward-facing within Kālarātri.
All the obstructors, wicked and terrifying, are beneath the soles of his feet.
His supreme face is white, red, and green;
he embraces Vārāhī, who is joined with him through the union of the vajra and bell.
Through the yoga of non-dual equality and the single flavor of all phenomena, he is indeed the one possessing the ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa), the glorious Mahāsukha-Vajra-Heruka.

He holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and carries a Dharma-wheel, a jharjhara drum, an alms-bowl, a trident, a noose, and a hook in his hands; likewise, he holds a severed head and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
With his left and right hands, he holds aloft a human skin garment.
In the east, however,
one should install these eight goddesses in their proper sequence: Mātaṅgī, Ḍombikā, Rajakī, Pukkasi, Khaṭṭikī, Śāvarī, Dhīvarī, and Śavarī.
Yellow, blue, and likewise red, born of smoky-grey color;
blood-red, green, smoke-colored, and white as the eighth;
thus are the Krodha-Ḍākinīs stationed at the gates.
Herukābhā, Vajracaṇḍī, and the supreme Vajrarākṣasī;
Vajrabhairavikā, the fierce one who devours all the unsubdued;
she who is white as ash and green, and terrifying with her red and blue [complexion].
In the center are eight [attributes]: a wheel of dharma, a jharjhara drum, a skull-cup, a ḍamaru drum, and a curved knife;
she wears her monastic robe over her shoulders; and at the gates are four goddesses.
[She holds] a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, the gesture of fearlessness, a shield, a jharjhara drum, and a ḍamaru drum.
They have one face and four arms, and stand upon a corpse-seat in the posture of half-lotus dance.

They are practitioners of the alms-round (*piṇḍapātika*), wearers of the three robes (*traicīvarika*), those who eat only after the midday meal (*paścātkhalubhaktika*), those who do not lie down (*naiṣadyika*), those who sleep wherever a mat is spread (*yathāsaṃstarika*), those who eat at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), those who dwell in the open air (*abhyavakāśika*), those who dwell at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*), those who dwell in the forest (*araṇyavāsika*), those who dwell in cemeteries (*śmaśānika*), those who wear robes made of rags from dust-heaps (*pāṃsukūlika*), and those who live on alms-food (*nāmantrika*). Thus, according to their sequence, the ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*) should be cultivated through purification. One should cultivate the state of the supreme single flavor of the knowledge-commitment (*jñāna-samaya*) and the commitment (*samaya*).
Oṃ śrī mahāsukhavajra he he ru ru kaṃ āḥ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ māṃ mātaṅgī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ ḍoṃ vajradombī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ raṃ rajakī hūṃ 2 phaṭ |
Oṃ puṃ pukkasī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ khaṃ khaṭṭikī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ sāṃ sāvarī hūṃ 2 phaṭ ||
Oṃ dhī dhīvarī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ heṃ saṃ savarī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ heṃ herukī hūṃ 2 phaṭ ||
Oṃ caṃ vajracaṇḍī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ rāṃ vajrarākṣasī hūṃ 2 phaṭ ||
Oṃ bheṃ bhairavī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
All these [goddesses] are naked with disheveled hair and three eyes;
they have gentle gazes and terrifying faces, their bodies adorned with the five mudrās,
and they wear crowns consisting of garlands of skulls.

Possessing the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) of laughter, tranquility, the erotic, the marvelous, the heroic, the loathsome, and the wrathful—free from anger—one should dwell in the movement of body, speech, and mind through recitation, meditative cultivation, emanation, and reabsorption. Because it brings about the attainment of the fruit of supreme gnosis through the enjoyment of sense objects that delight and gladden beings according to their various inclinations by means of skillful methods for training them, and because beings thereby enjoy the nectar face-to-face and obtain the fruit of attaining gnosis, it is the "state of having obtained the boon" for all sentient beings.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the Chapter on the Arising of the Qualities of Austerity (*dhutaguṇa*), in the *Abhidhānottara-tantra*. || 1214' ||
